question:
Patient note:
A 46-year-old man is evaluated this morning in the orthopaedic theatre holding bay for an urgently arranged left knee arthroscopy that the sports-medicine consultant estimates will last 40 minutes under general anaesthesia; the intention is to trim a displaced bucket-handle tear of the medial meniscus that has repeatedly locked the joint in 30 degrees of flexion. Since sustaining an anterior-chest squeezing pain nineteen days ago that proved to be an ST-segment elevation infarction of the inferior wall, he has remained on the cardiac telemetry ward, and nursing documentation shows he has not taken more than a handful of assisted pivot transfers to a bedside chair during the entire admission—physical therapy has deferred hallway ambulation until after today’s procedure because of his ongoing reliance on continuous ECG monitoring and intravenous nitroglycerin during the first week. Coronary angiography performed on the day of the infarct revealed an acute thrombotic occlusion of the mid-right coronary artery successfully treated with a drug-eluting stent; ventricular function is preserved with an ejection fraction of 55 %, and he has had no episodes of pulmonary congestion, orthopnoea, or lower-extremity oedema since the event. The cardiology team transitioned him from heparin to dual antiplatelet therapy three days after the intervention, and his most recent high-sensitivity troponin has trended down to 24 ng L⁻¹ from a peak of 7,800 ng L⁻¹. The current orthopaedic problem predates his cardiac event by several months but became intolerable during convalescence when he could no longer compensate with quadriceps strength or bracing. His oncologic history includes a resected stage II sigmoid adenocarcinoma four years ago for which he completed twelve cycles of adjuvant FOLFOX; surveillance colonoscopy six months ago was clear, CT chest–abdomen–pelvis last quarter showed no recurrence, and he has been off chemotherapy for over three years, carrying no implanted ports or catheters at present. He has not required any surgical procedures since that colon resection, and there have been no operations within the past 30 days. He denies fevers, rigors, sputum production, or any diagnosed pneumonia or bloodstream infection during the current stay, and there have been no recent splints, casts, or traction devices on either lower limb. Review of systems is negative for paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, wheeze, chronic cough, exertional syncope, transient focal neurologic deficits, bowel disturbance suggestive of inflammatory disease, or chronic steroid use. He denies any prior cerebrovascular accident or transient ischaemic attack, and has sustained no major trauma, fractures of the hip, pelvis, or leg, or spinal cord injury leading to paralysis during this admission or in the preceding month. He recalls no prior deep venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolus, or unexplained clotting episodes among first-degree relatives. Pre-procedure examination finds him supine with the head of bed elevated 20 degrees; he converses easily, is oriented, and reports mild substernal soreness but no active chest pain. Vital signs twenty minutes ago: temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 126/74 mm Hg, heart rate 68 beats min⁻¹ in regular sinus rhythm, respirations 14 min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air. Neck veins are not distended; carotid upstrokes are brisk; S₁ and S₂ are crisp without added sounds or murmurs. Lungs are clear bilaterally. Abdomen is soft and nontender with a well-healed left lower-quadrant laparotomy scar. The operative knee is held in partial flexion with palpable joint-line tenderness and moderate effusion; distal pulses are 2 + and symmetric, calves are supple without cord, pitting, or visible varicosities, and circumference 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity measures 37 cm on each side. Skin over both forearms reveals a single 18-gauge peripheral cannula in the right cephalic vein running lactated Ringer’s at keep-open rate; no central access devices are present. He has never experienced heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and platelet counts have remained within the reference range throughout this hospitalization. Laboratory studies drawn at 05:00 show haemoglobin 14.2 g dL⁻¹, haematocrit 42 %, platelet count 235 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, leukocytes 6.8 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 138 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.1 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 23 mmol L⁻¹, creatinine 0.97 mg dL⁻¹, AST 24 U L⁻¹, ALT 22 U L⁻¹, total bilirubin 0.7 mg dL⁻¹, prothrombin time 12.3 s with an international normalised ratio of 1.1, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. A 12-lead ECG reviewed by anaesthesia shows normal sinus rhythm at 66 beats min⁻¹, Q waves in leads III and aVF consistent with the recent infarct, and no acute ST deviation. Posterior–anterior chest radiograph obtained yesterday demonstrates clear lung fields, normal mediastinal silhouette, and well-expanded lungs without pleural effusion. Body mass index is 26 kg m⁻². He has been nil per os since midnight, removed his own dentures and jewellery, and pneumatic compression sleeves were applied but remain deflated until induction. Antithrombotic pharmacological prophylaxis has been withheld pending operative haemostasis and coordination with cardiology regarding perioperative management of his dual antiplatelet regimen.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
Using the duration-based Caprini VTE score, add the applicable preoperative risk factors:
- Age 46 (41–60 years) = 1.
- BMI 26 (>25 kg/m²) = 1.
- Planned 40-minute arthroscopy: minor surgery lasting <45 minutes = 1. Count the operation once.
- Myocardial infarction 19 days ago (within 1 month) = 1.
- Bed confinement for ≥72 hours: 19 days with only assisted chair transfers = 2.
- Prior malignancy: resected sigmoid cancer still counts despite remission = 2.
No additional points are documented for heart failure, prior VTE, thrombophilia, cast, major fracture, or central venous access. The peripheral IV does not qualify.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 8.
Final answer: 8
